The twenty-sixth year of the Republic: the War of Resistance. In fallen Tianjin there arose an “Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps.” Of this band of young men the writer has again and again dwelt upon their purity and their sincerity, upon their hearts brimming with ardor and their whole-souled, wholehearted patriotic loyalty. Such praise is in no way overdone; and one thing more must be added: the valor of these young men sprang wholly from their own kindling and their own resolve—it was by no means pumped into them from without.

Ten years later, in the thirty-sixth year of the Republic: the suppression of rebellion. The trainees of the “Lizhi Class,” who after a short course of training at Nanjing were straightway dispatched to the twenty-odd provinces of North and Central China, were of the same purity, the same plain honesty, the same indifference alike to fame and to gain as the members of that old “Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps.” Most precious of all, they did not carry “sacrifice and devotion” forever upon their lips, mouthing it merely as a slogan, but made it manifest in deeds actually done.

Ten years more, twenty years, down to the present day, and the background of the age, the shape of society, the scale of values have all undergone drastic change—the culture lagging behind while the economy has run on ahead—so that the run of young men now incline for the most part toward the utilitarian, and are no longer what they were in those days. This is but a stirring of feeling amid old memories; I have no mind here to argue right and wrong.
In the foregoing chapter and in this one, the fall of Shijiazhuang is twice set down. In both places mention is made of how ill-matched in numbers were the two sides, the attacking and the defending.

By how much, exactly, did they differ? At a rough reckoning, about a ratio of one to ten. Our army had but a single division and a few peace-preservation units, no more than 10,000 men in all; whereas the bandit army had, after its reorganization, seven columns, a host of some 100,000. From this one may see how urgently the Chinese Communist Central Committee sought to take Shijiazhuang and make of it a second Yan’an. Thereafter, all through the year and more until the fall of Beiping, Shijiazhuang was the seat from which the Chinese Communists issued their commands.

Our unit had, in the near suburbs of the northeastern corner of Beiping, disposed a “North-Suburb Mixed Group,” and afterward, in the scenic district of Beiping’s western suburbs, disposed a “West-Suburb Mixed Group” besides. Both places lay under the ceaseless harassment of the Chinese Communist militia, and were the very spots where pacification work was needed; yet, merely for the difference in the working ground, the upshot was that in the one place we were greatly welcomed, and in the other met with rejection. What passed all expectation was that they who spurned us came from our own side of the line.

Under the “North-Suburb Group” there was an “intelligence squad,” made up of a dozen men and more; and because of the bandit army’s frequent raids it was fitted out with equipment of the heavier firepower. On the night of the eve of the Double-Tenth Festival in the thirty-seventh year, the bandit army came on in force with three militia brigades, a thousand men and more; our “intelligence squad,” joining with the local self-defense brigade of a hundred and more, went out to meet them, and a pitched slaughter began. From nine o’clock at night it was fought clear through to the dawn of the next day, a grapple that lasted in all a dozen hours and more; and when the field was cleared after the battle, the dead and wounded lay strewn on every hand, a sight too dreadful to look upon.

This piece, the “Battle of Lishuiqiao,” gives in its text a close account of the actions, such as, save for one who lived through it and came alive out of a hopeless pass, one could hardly conceive of. The latter part of the original, in the scene it set down of the field after the battle, was too pitiful; the writer has left out a few short passages—for, thinking it over, it was the common people of the place, when all is said, who suffered the ravage.
Following upon the last section of the fourth chapter, here again is an account touching the state of things after the fall of Shijiazhuang.

Our First Brigade and the Second Section of the “Beiping Field Headquarters,” besides their fixed liaison, had also a coordination in the work. That is to say, apart from the directly subordinate “Shimen Work-Group,” there was besides a “directly subordinate member” attached to the working unit which the Field Headquarters’ Second Section had posted at Shimen; and this fellow-worker was none other than my fellow-student Lu Deming, who furnished the account “How the Communist Bandits Mounted Their Great Invasion of Shimen in the Winter of the Thirty-Sixth Year.”
What follows is the original text of this account; its matter does not overlap with the “Brief Record of the Work at Shijiazhuang” furnished by my fellow-student Niu Guangjin.

“One. The general state of the garrison troops and of the guard and peace-preservation forces at that time. (1) The Third Army, its commander Luo Lirong, had under it two divisions; the designation of one division I fail to recall, the other being the 32nd Division, its commander Li Wending and its deputy commander Liu Ying. The army commander Luo led the main body in a northward withdrawal as far as Wangdu, and after fierce fighting was taken prisoner.

“(2) The post of Shimen garrison commander was held concurrently by the 32nd Division commander Li Wending, and that of deputy garrison commander concurrently by the deputy division commander Liu Ying; they held Shijiazhuang fast.
“(3) The chief of the police bureau Liu Qingchi, the chief inspector Zhao Jinjun, and the rest maintained the local public order and joined in the defense.
“(4) The peace-preservation commander Hou Zigu directed the civilian militia.

“Two. An estimate of the Communist forces. (1) The forces under Nie Rongzhen of the ‘Jin-Cha-Ji Military District,’ amounting to some three columns, together with a certain number of directly subordinate units.
“(2) The several ‘Military District’ forces belonging to the ‘Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu Border Region,’ together with the four columns under the command of Yang Dezhi, Yang Chengwu, and the rest.

(The writer’s note: In the year and more from the winter of the thirty-sixth year to the beginning of the thirty-eighth year, the “establishment” and “designations” of the Communist army were at their most confused. Broadly, all their forces were divided into three grades—“field forces,” “military-district forces,” and “guerrilla forces”—though the actual tendency was for the “field forces” to grow ever more numerous, while the “guerrilla forces” dwindled by degrees to nothing.

By that time the Chinese Communists, in their wholesale revolt, had cast aside and left unused the formal military designation the government had conferred upon them—the “Eighteenth Group Army”—and had gone so far as to style themselves the “People’s Liberation Army.”

From the eleventh month of the thirty-sixth year, the main body of the Communist army invading Shimen was made up of the “field forces” and “military-district forces” belonging to the “Jin-Cha-Ji People’s Liberation Army” and to Nie Rongzhen’s “Jin-Cha-Ji Military District.” And this designation, “Jin-Cha-Ji People’s Liberation Army,” after being used no great while, was changed again to “North China People’s Liberation Army.”

The Chinese Communist “Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu Border Region” was first got up by the forces of Liu Bocheng, the 129th Division of the Eighth Route Army. It lay in the linking belt along the borders of the four provinces of Shanxi, Hebei, Shandong, and Henan, set between the two great mountain ranges of the Taihang and the Taiyue. For the convenience of command, the Chinese Communists divided this border region into two strategic units, namely the “Jin-Ji-Yu Border Region” and the “Ji-Lu-Yu Border Region.”

The “Jin-Ji-Yu Border Region” took in the southeastern part of Shanxi province and a small part of Henan province north of the Yellow River; on the east it reached to the Ping-Han railway, where it met the Ji-Lu-Yu region; on the south it ran to the Yellow River, and on the north to the Zheng-Tai railway, where it met the Jin-Cha-Ji Border Region.
The “Ji-Lu-Yu Border Region” took in the southern part of Hebei province, the western part of Shandong province, the region north of Henan, and a small part of Jiangsu north of the Long-Hai railway.

Its four bounds were these: on the east it reached to the Jin-Pu railway, adjoining the Shandong “base area”; on the west to the Ping-Han railway, meeting the “Jin-Ji-Yu region”; on the north to the De-Shi railway (from Dezhou in Shandong to Shimen in Hebei), bordering the “Central Hebei region”; and on the south it ran to the Long-Hai railway. All these territories were such as the Communist army had seized bit by bit during the War of Resistance, while the national army fought the Japanese and the Communist army tripped it from behind. Taking only the four-province border region of Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu, the Communist army held fourteen county towns and a certain number of townships, an area of about 600,000 square li, with a population of some 25,000,000.

Strictly speaking, the “Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu Border Region” was a rebel “administrative organ,” its full name being the “Government Council of the Jin-Ji-Lu-Yu Border Region” (its bogus chairman Yang Xiufeng, its bogus vice-chairman Bo Yibo). Within the region were divided a number of “military districts,” and a part of the Communist force that this time attacked Shimen belonged to the “South Hebei Military District.”) Here ends the writer’s note; what follows is again the original text of my fellow-student Lu, resuming the “estimate of the Communist forces.” (3) Besides the several columns listed above, there were the local militia as well; set against our national army, the enemy was many and we were few—out of all proportion, in very truth.

“Three. The posture of our army. (1) Bound by the fetters of the ‘Political Consultation,’ by the bandit side’s ruse of ‘now halting, now fighting,’ and by the takeover grandees who enjoyed to the full the ‘fruits of victory,’ our army was mocked as the ‘Strip-It-Clean Force,’ and its fighting spirit was wholly gone.

“(2) The people’s hearts were not with us—yet toward the Communist bandits they harbored a wariness; only the local self-defense corps had a will to fight of the fiercest. But their firearms were old past use, and though they battled to the death, in the end they were put to death by the bandit army and the bandit cadres.

“(3) After the fall of Shimen it appeared there had been great stores of firearms and ammunition in the depots, which in the fighting were never even issued out for the self-defense corps to use; in the confusion they were set off in an explosion, and a great fire burned a whole day and night, its embers not dying out.

“Four. The savage doings of the bandit army after they had stormed the place. (1) The political commissar of the ‘Jin-Cha-Ji Military District,’ Huang Jing (that is, Yu Qiwei), after the Communist army had usurped Shimen, was the first to hold the post of chairman of the ‘Shimen Military Control Commission,’ and before long was transferred to be ‘mayor of Shimen city.’

“(2) A proclamation of the ‘Shimen Military Control Commission’: that all former public servants and teachers were with all speed to carry out a ‘self-surrender registration’ and be brought under ‘control.’

“(3) A week later the city of Shimen set up a ‘Public Security Bureau,’ which searched house by house; all the young and able-bodied were, without exception, taken off to sundry places of concentration and there held, and when night came were moved again to another secret place to be examined one by one. Along the way of removal there went a great throng of bandit troops and puppet police, bayonets fixed and rounds in the chamber, keeping strict guard the whole road.
“(4) After about half a month, word came without cease that many persons had already been executed.

“(5) Within the countless concentration camps, great and small, there were ‘planted’ Communist spies who by every art drew out men’s talk. Any who showed discontent, who let fall a word of complaint, who disclosed his own standing, or who was reckoned gravely suspect—such as the so-called ‘Nationalist agents,’ ‘wicked despot landlords,’ ‘idlers,’ and the like—were at any moment haled off for questioning or shifted to another place, and whether they thereafter lived or died was never known.

“(6) Those generally deemed of lighter case—who in truth were altogether ‘innocent’—were held in the larger concentration places; save that now and then a copy or two of the ‘People’s Daily’ and the ‘Liberation Army Daily’ would be dealt out and read aloud to them by a ‘public security man,’ they had scarcely any activity out of doors.

“As for their food—millet gruel or sorghum-rice, one bowl a meal, with a little vegetable and never a scrap of meat or fish—it was not near enough to fill the belly. And the privy-pits (the latrines) were set within the very wooden pales that penned the men; it was well the weather was cold, for had it been summer, the thing would have been past all imagining.

“(7) But there was worse than this, and it lay in the life of the spirit. The bandit cadres set to watch over them would open their mouths only to say, ‘You have wronged the people; do not waste the people’s grain,’ and shut them only to say, ‘You are steeped in guilt from head to foot; you could not redeem it in a lifetime.’ There was no fixed term to a man’s being haled up or let go; his life and death hung upon a passing whim of the bandit cadres; and dwelling every hour and moment in terror and despair—how bitter such days were to live through!

“(8) It is commonly said that the Communists are ‘loose’ in the relations of men and women; but little do people know how utterly ‘wanton’ they are in the handling of those relations. There was once a middle-aged man and woman, husband and wife, whose marriage was not as it should be, and who were actually paraded through the streets for a show: the woman went in front, holding up a ‘worn shoe,’ and had to cry aloud without ceasing, ‘This worn shoe of mine has done wrong’; the man went in the middle of the procession, a ‘night-pot’ hung about his neck, and cried likewise, ‘I do so love to smell the reek of lust’; while the bandit cadres brought up the rear, whips in hand, now as though driving cattle, now bawling out, ‘I do so love to meddle in this business that is none of mine.’ Only think what a scene this was—not a shred of human dignity to be spoken of; and by this one may catch a glimpse of their savagery.” (The writer’s note: In the foregoing there are certain terms peculiar to the Communists, and several bits of local slang that the Communists have made yet uglier, which I here set forth briefly as follows.—By “Nationalist agent” is meant a secret operative of the Nationalist party, whom the Communists regarded as their foremost enemy. Upon any who opposed them in political thought, or who were not Communist, they would, wishing to fasten a crime, clap without distinction this cap of “Nationalist agent”; and in the time of the great “Red Guard” uproar, even their own “state chairman” Liu Shaoqi became a “Nationalist agent.”

An “idler” (in some places also called a “ne’er-do-well”) is the sort of lounging, do-nothing local ruffian and rogue. “Worn shoe” is a name used in certain counties of Shanxi, Chahar, and Suiyuan for a “secret whore”; it is at the same time a phrase that demeans a woman’s character and reviles a person as base, the sense being that this shoe has been worn by many and is already worn through—Shijiazhuang lies near Shanxi, and so the term is current there. A “night-pot” is the chamber-pot used at night; in years past in the north, the weather being cold, folk who were neither old nor ailing would use one all the same, to be spared rising in the night and taking a chill; it serves too as a means of mocking a person, though one seldom hears it now.) So much for the recollection and after-record set down by my fellow-student Lu Deming, forty years after the fall of Shimen. Read together with the “Brief Record of the Work at Shijiazhuang” written by my fellow-student Niu Guangjin in the fourth chapter, it may be the more worth the seeing. The writer feels this: that to write of a temper in which battle after battle is won brings, even where one had no part oneself, a sense of elation and delight; whereas to set down defeat upon defeat cannot but bring some measure of vexation and low spirits. So it is with me; how it may be with others, I do not know.
Perhaps it is for this reason that in “biographies” and in “war histories” the battles won are many, and the battles lost are few.

In the near suburbs of Beiping we disposed a somewhat larger “North-Suburb Mixed Group.” The North Suburb is the northern outskirts of the city of Beiping; but in fact the working range of the “North-Suburb Mixed Group” took in as well parts of the counties of Daxing and Changping in Hebei province.

The group’s first leader, though he came out of the “Japanese Military Academy,” was likewise a trainee of the “Lizhi Class.” At that time he was six or seven years older than the run of his fellow-students, and so had the more experience behind him.

Until he said so, and I could not myself recall it, it turned out that back in the twenty-seventh year of the Republic he had already been my pupil. My fellow-student Chang Shaozeng (who came out of the Japanese Military Academy) furnished a piece of reference material, wherein were a few brief passages of record.—“One. Touching the course of my joining the ‘North China Loyal and Patriotic Army Cadre Training Class’: ‘That year (the spring of the twenty-seventh), toward ten in the forenoon, I and Qian Zhilun, Wang Zhong, Yin Donggeng, Yan Shangxin, and a dozen more in all, each took a train and came to Tianjin. That very day we lodged in the ‘Shude Primary School’ within the British Concession and began to undergo training; every movement was carried on under the strictest secrecy, that our whereabouts might not be laid open.’

“‘In the training class the subjects of study were ‘guerrilla tactics,’ ‘intelligence,’ ‘reconnaissance,’ ‘the exposition of demolition,’ ‘horsemanship,’ and further ‘talks on the spirit,’ ‘analysis of current affairs,’ and the like.’

“‘That school was in its winter vacation, with no teachers and not a pupil to be seen; we had our lessons by day and held our exercises by night, and who the instructors were that came to teach us, none of us knew.’
“‘One night several strangers came all at once, and forthwith led us in taking an oath, smearing our lips with blood to join the ‘Renaissance Society.’

“We all knelt before the portrait of the Party Leader and the flags of the party and the state, and one by one read out the words of the oath, the sum of which was: ‘In all sincerity I enter in; with fixed resolve I shall keep this forever; should I break my oath, I willingly bear a heavy punishment.’ ‘In the British Concession at Tianjin there was a racecourse (races of the gambling kind), and two or three of us at a time were taken by turns to practice riding, paying only some small fee by the hour. This was the activity that interested us most. Next to it were the discussion meetings held indoors.’

“‘The two weeks of training were in a twinkling at an end, and we were straightway dispatched, in secret and each apart—some to the cities, some to the countryside—parting from one another without a word, much in the mood of that old line, ‘The wind blows bleak.’’

“(The writer’s note: The forerunner of the ‘North China Loyal and Patriotic Army’ was the ‘Luan-Yu Guerrilla General Headquarters’; both these units were organs of the resistance against Japan. In my capacity as chief of the ‘Tianjin Station of the Juntong Bureau,’ I held concurrently, at one time and another, the post of deputy commander of both these organizations.

“My fellow-student Chang Shaozeng speaks of the ‘Cadre Training Class’; though it was got up by the ‘North China Loyal and Patriotic Army,’ it was in its actual business presided over by the ‘Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps’ led by my comrade Zeng Che, secretary of the ‘Tianjin Station.’ The cadres under training, too, came for the most part from the ‘Traitor-Killing Corps.’

“I myself went to the ‘Shude Primary School’ to give them lessons, and to deliver talks on the spirit besides. My one impression was that these patriotic young men were, every one, innocent, pure, and lovable. In that age they did not yet know what was meant by ‘sacrifice and devotion,’ nor did they carry ‘sacrifice and devotion’ upon their lips as a slogan; yet in all they did, beyond the supremacy of state and nation, there was never a thought of self.) ‘Two. The political work of the Third Route Army of the ‘North China Loyal and Patriotic Army’: ‘The district in which this guerrilla force was active was the countryside about Pingyuan county and Yucheng county in Shandong province.’

“‘After my graduation from the ‘Cadre Training Class,’ I went, with the liaison staff-officer Mr. Liu sent from the Shandong district, on foot by way of Dezhou to the headquarters of the ——th Regiment of the ‘Third Route Army of the Loyal and Patriotic Army,’ and forthwith joined the guerrilla ranks. All of us were high in the temper of resistance, sallying out often; the wrecking of railways and highways was our regular charge. I remember that once on a highway we valiantly seized two Japanese military trucks and three drivers; and on questioning them one by one we found they were all of Korean birth, whereupon our enmity at once vanished, and they too were willing to serve our army in the transport work. At that time the ‘Third Route of the Loyal and Patriotic Army’ had a ‘forward office’ set up in the town of Pingyuan county, under cover of a shop; the man in charge of it was Mr. Wang —— (his name I forget), said to be of the ‘Young China Party,’ who took a lively concern in our work.’
“‘Before long, sundry Chinese Communist guerrilla bands also infiltrated this district, and from that time forth friction arose without cease between them and our army.’

“(The writer’s note: As for the ‘Third Route Army of the North China Loyal and Patriotic Army’ in Shandong, I recall only that it was managed by my friend Wang Fuzhou; the particulars of it I do not rightly know.

“That man of the Young China Party whose name my fellow-student Chang Shaozeng forgot was very likely my friend Wang Fuzhou. Wang Fuzhou, also called Wang Zhenwu, a man of Henan, a delegate to the National Assembly, once served in Taiwan as vice-minister of economic affairs. He had a passage of turning from foe to friend with the ‘Juntong Bureau,’ and that was in the days of my tenure as chief of the ‘Beiping Station.’ Now my friend Fuzhou has been dead these many years, and there is no more chance to talk over with him this dramatic old affair.) ‘Three. Transferred from the ‘Third Route Army’ in Shandong to the ‘Ninth Route Army’ in East Hebei: ‘Its station was in the wild country about Linnancang in Baodi county and Yutian county in Hebei province. Its commander was Wang Wen, its chief of staff Qi Qingbin, and the head of its political department Zhang Kexin (that is, Zhang Zuoxing). There were besides Chen Zhaoji and Luo Yongkang, who had come forward to volunteer from the ‘Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps,’ and the head of the wireless station, and others.’

“‘The force stationed at Linnancang numbered about a thousand men and more; and there were besides small detachments scattered through the several villages, a hundred or two apiece. Their regular charge was, severally, to seize the chance to strike at the enemy and the puppets, and to wreck the transport and the communications.’

“‘On the far bank across the river there was a body of Chinese Communist troops, some one hundred to two hundred strong, clad in ill-kept green uniforms, who in the posture of a ‘friendly force’ sent over two so-called political cadres to ‘pay a visit.’ On the collars of their uniforms were stamped the English letters ‘CP,’ a thing truly neither fish nor fowl. These two, seeing our work-progress chart, praised it greatly, and even made a point of copying one out to take away, saying they wished to learn from us. Our headquarters, though it kept a wariness of them, could only meet them with a show of civility on the surface, since the government had after all called upon all to ‘join in resisting Japan.’ ‘One day two or three ‘heroic personages’ came down to us; they were all men who, after the sanction carried out upon Wang Kemin in Beiping, had slipped away from the scene and made their roundabout way back to the base at Linnancang to rejoin their ranks, and one of them was even wounded. To hear them talk freely of how the thing had gone at the time filled one with admiration unbounded.’

“‘I remember that once, toward dusk, the force was mustered, and a dozen picked and able men and more were chosen out, disguised in the guise of merchants and boatmen but each still bearing a weapon hidden, and in parties boarded two great wooden boats and set off for Tianjin. The errand of this journey, it turned out, was to take delivery of a consignment of arms, among them rifles, pistols, and ammunition. The two great wooden boats, looking as though laden with country produce, followed the other craft and slipped quietly along the Grand Canal into a little wharf. This was likely within the Concessions, though whether it was the British or the French Concession could no longer be made out in the dark of night.’

“‘Because the preparation beforehand had been full enough, and the ‘loading’ was done with the nimblest dispatch, in no long while the lading was finished and we weighed anchor at once and put out. But who could have known—we had not gone far when someone on the bank shouted an order to halt for inspection; our boat, of course, could not stop to be searched, and those on the bank, seeing their shouts of no avail, forthwith fired a warning shot; we were forced to return the fire, and at the same time made all haste to speed northward back along the way we had come, into the Grand Canal, and returned to our former post.’ (The writer’s note: The commander of the ‘North China Loyal and Patriotic Ninth Route Army’ was held concurrently by Wang Wen, leader of the ‘Tianjin Station Action Group’; this force too was a mainstay of the North China Loyal and Patriotic Army, and so the ‘headquarters’ chief of staff Qi Qingbin and the head of its political department Zhang Kexin (Zuoxing) at the same time held concurrently the posts of chief of staff and head of the political department of the ‘Ninth Route Army.’

“On the collars of the Chinese Communist guerrillas’ garb were worn the two English letters ‘CP,’ signifying that they were of the ‘Chinese Communist Party.’ This was already a thing of the early days of the War of Resistance; thereafter it was never seen again, for they had gone into the dark and dared no more show themselves by any emblem. In the case of the sanction carried out upon Wang Kemin in Meizha Hutong at Beiping, the brave men who took part were, one and all, picked out by the action-group leader Wang Wen from the headquarters at Baodi; after the affair there were dead and there were wounded—for the fuller account see the last chapter of the first of these poor books.
“For the doings of the ‘Ninth Route Army’ about East Hebei, see the first chapter of the second of these poor books.

“The three fragments set down above by my fellow-student Chang Shaozeng all bear upon the work I once presided over, and set side by side they have the more interest.) Now I should come to the ‘North-Suburb Mixed Group.’ Why was it called a ‘Mixed Group’? Even I myself cannot say.

The passage below was likewise furnished by the group’s leader, my fellow-student Chang Shaozeng, and I set down his original text hereafter. ‘One. A brief sketch of the ‘North-Suburb Mixed Group’: ‘After we had been trained at Nanjing and dispatched to Beiping, the forming and sending out of the ‘North-Suburb Mixed Group’ may be reckoned among the later batches. This band had officers but no rank and file—twenty-two men in the whole group, all of them college and higher-school youths, and among them some, having a little experience, from the ‘Youth Army,’ who had asked to be transferred over for the training; skilled alike in letters and in arms, they set one another off to advantage.’

“‘That forenoon the deputy brigade commander Mr. Li Yulin led the whole of our twenty-two members, carrying our provisions and baggage, out of the city (by Dongzhimen) in large jeeps, and we reached the ‘village of Zhaojiafen’ at the northeastern corner of Beiping. At that time the several villages of this tract, though they suffered harassment, were still tolerably quiet, and might be said to be yet under our own governance.’

“‘We left our provisions and baggage in the keeping of the village head, and the whole group at once set off northward in light order to learn the state of things. After going twenty li and more, and passing ‘Lishuiqiao,’ we had entered the gray zone where the bandit troops and bandit cadres came and went from time to time, which some also call a ‘district of the three unmanaged.’’
“‘Patrolling in parties, we found no trace of the other side; we saw only a scene of utter desolation, the common folk shrinking and cowering—it moved us to a double grief.’
“‘On the walls everywhere were daubed slogans written by the bandit cadres, such as ‘On every scrap and corner of ground, plant much squash and beans’ (the character ai read wo) and the like.’

“(The writer’s note: This slogan, ‘On every scrap and corner of ground, plant much squash and beans,’ looks on the face of it to be an urging to make use of every inch of soil and to further the growing of crops. In truth, however, whenever they came into a village, they always scoured up the people’s food, and whatever was eatable, careless whether the folk lived or died, they carried off all they could lift. So that the more the farm households planted, the more it served their turn to take. The ‘ai gourd’ is the pumpkin; in the countryside about Beiping a largish pumpkin of a dozen catties and more is nothing rare. Of beans there are several kinds, the common sort being long cowpeas and hyacinth beans. The string beans now often seen in the Taiwan markets were not yet in Beiping forty years ago; and where one chanced to see them, they were a variant sort, which people called ‘foreign hyacinth beans.’) ‘After we came back from our reconnaissance, we took ‘Zhaojiafen’ and ‘Beihuqu’ for our bases and began to open up the pacification work. First we set up ‘mutual-aid bands,’ every household providing itself with firearms, patrolling day and night, posting watches at the key points, village passing word to village, each busy at his own task. In less than three months the mustering and drilling of the populace had already taken some shape, and from that time the petty rogues went into hiding, and the district grew daily more settled.’

“(The writer’s note: The common people of the place could by no means afford to buy guns, nor was there any place to buy them. The particulars I no longer recall very clearly, but in the main the arms for mustering and drilling the local self-defense were for the most part supplied by the brigade headquarters. Their source was that lot of arms which the Japanese army had surrendered and handed over, brought back from Tianjin—for which see the third chapter above.) ‘The brigade commander requested Mr. Zheng Enpu to recommend fifteen assault men of proven fighting experience, who under the command of Tian Yingjie were formed under the name of the ‘North-Suburb Mixed Group Intelligence Squad,’ and took up their post at ‘Lishuiqiao’ as a strongpoint, pushing forward by degrees to the north. Before long they had recovered the northern tract of ‘Lishuiqiao,’ and the Communist bandits’ sundry guerrilla bands, together with the militia of no fixed form, all fled away northward.’

“‘One day an old man from the eastern hamlet of ‘Zhaojiafen’ came to the force bearing the better half of a bottle of sesame oil. He said: ‘You brothers toil too hard, running about for the district by day and by night alike; it truly weighs on my mind. We got a bottle of oil at home, and, grudging it to ourselves to eat, share the half with you. The thing is little enough, but it speaks a small corner of my heart.’ These two remarks were truly moving; there was nothing for it but to take the old man’s half-bottle of sesame oil, and to give him back in return a sack of ten catties or so of the white rice we used for our mess; and the old man went off with it on his back, chuckling merrily.’

“‘That the district had taken on some life was, when all is said, a good thing. The Civil Affairs Bureau of the Beiping Municipal Government sent men specially to bring us their solace, bearing a horizontal streamer of red cloth on which was written ‘Welcome to Unit 0760 for a Long Stay.’ And so the ‘North-Suburb Group’ won itself a name in this tract. Of course we did not grow complacent at it; only think—our whole brigade was but a few hundred on the roll, and with twenty-two mainstay men we had brought pacification to but two or three villages; even if this be an achievement, it was a very limited one.’ Below I set down further a fragment on the ‘West-Suburb Mixed Group.’ This too was furnished by my fellow-student Chang Shaozeng, his text running as follows.—‘In the spring of the thirty-seventh year I suddenly received an order from the brigade headquarters transferring me to the western suburb of the city to set up yet another ‘West-Suburb Mixed Group.’ This ‘West-Suburb Group’ was made up of Xiao Runyu and thirteen others, fourteen in all, its seat next to the ‘Haidian’ district office outside Xizhimen.’

“‘The western suburb means the tract from outside Beiping’s Xizhimen all the way to the ‘Western Hills’ and ‘Wanshou Hill,’ reaching south toward ‘Mentougou’ and joining on the north the ‘Ming Tombs’ and ‘Badaling’—a wide expanse, a stretch of hill country running on for scores of li.’

“‘The dwellers here were of a high degree of culture, and their standard of living was passable too, not so poor and backward as in the North Suburb. Because the ‘Youth Army’s 208th Division’ was garrisoned there, the bandit crew dared not act openly and barefaced in this tract, and so the district was comparatively at peace.’

“‘We once paid a visit to the headquarters of the ‘208th Division,’ where the chief of staff came out to receive us, and his very first word was to ask me: ‘Is your group’s line of work turned inward? or outward?’ At these words of his I could not but be taken aback: the fate of the nation was already come to its trial, and how should a general of station so high as his still harbor a thought of this kind?’

“‘The common folk of the western suburb, hearing that we had come from the North Suburb, treated us with an especial warmth and cordiality. But here the government offices were many, and the work was hard to carry forward smoothly. Here too we met with an amusing thing: the celebrated player of the national opera Cheng Yanqiu (Yanqiu) lived at a spot not too far from us, and several times he walked over to chat, and to discourse at length on the ‘origins of the drama’; he said he was a good friend of our unit commander Mr. Chen, and that he had long looked up to our unit as well, and he hoped we would come and go the more; once or twice he even went along with our brothers to view the ancient sites.’

“One day the brigade headquarters sent a man with an order, the sum of which was: ‘The several inspection posts sent out by the West-Suburb Group are herewith to be withdrawn at once....’ Turning it over, it was very likely that we had not clearly grasped the working ground, and had misused the working method, and thereby incurred the dissatisfaction of the other units.
“And the ‘West-Suburb Mixed Group’ was thereupon withdrawn.

The writer’s note: One. The sending out of this ‘West-Suburb Mixed Group’ was, just as my fellow-student Chang Shaozeng says, undertaken without our having at all clearly grasped the working ground, and I too own that it was a mistaken decision. The chief thing was this: the ‘North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters’ was seated in the very western suburb, and this business of ours they could not abide the sight of—would not, of course, accept it, and felt withal always in their hearts that we were an ‘eyesore.’ Not to speak of Fu Zuoyi, whose sense of turf ran the stronger and who was ill at ease over it, even the Youth Army of the Central line must needs ask what was ‘inward’ and what ‘outward’—a thing simply past all comprehending.

Two. Cheng Yanqiu said that he and I were good friends; in fact it was not so, though there is, to tell it, a story behind it. In the twenty-second year of the Republic I lived alone by myself in Shenbizi Hutong at Beiping, in a house shared out on lease—one large room and one small. By day I went to my office on Beichang Street, and at night came back to sleep. At that time I was chief of the ‘Beiping Station,’ and of those who knew where I lodged there was only my friend Bai Shiwei, and I had no intercourse with the outside world at all.

My landlord, surnamed Zhang, was a man of the roving brotherhood; he had no notion of what I did, but now and then he would ask me over for a meal and a chat. Seeing that we were young, and neither burly nor strong, he urged us to practice the martial arts, and would even present us to a master.
His house was very roomy, and the honored guest who lodged with him was none other than old Mr. Du Xinwu of Cili in Hunan, a man of the highest repute and great name in his day.

Old Mr. Du not only carried within him consummate skills, but bestrode both brotherhoods, though he would not lightly display himself. In the Hongmen he was the ‘dragon head’ of ‘Qixia Mountain’; in the Green Gang his standing was of the ‘twenty-first’ generation, that is, what is commonly called the ‘Da-character generation.’

At the first, old Mr. Du agreed only to take us as ‘disciples,’ and would not accept the ‘great ceremonial obeisance.’ At that time there were but two of us: besides myself, the other was Cheng Yanqiu. A tie of this kind can only, and barely, be called that of ‘brothers under one master.’ Afterward, for reasons of the work, I moved house, and we had no further contact. As to whether Cheng Yanqiu in later days entered fully into old Mr. Du’s chambers—that I do not know.

From the twenty-second year to the thirty-sixth I had no dealings at all with Cheng, and even while I was in Beiping I did not care to see Cheng’s plays. After I came back to Beiping in the thirty-sixth year, I lodged for hire in Dongguanyinsi Hutong, when one day, all unlooked-for, Cheng came to my house to see me and talk over old times; I kept him to a meal, and he was not only a great talker but a mighty drinker. As to how he had come to know where I lodged, I did not closely ask.

After this he came several times more, and every time it was to plead a favor: either some kinsman of his had been seized by the ‘North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,’ or the son of a servant in his household, caught up by ‘implication,’ was held in the ‘Inspection Office’; and he hoped I would come forward to ‘stand surety.’ But when I made inquiry, it turned out that all of them were ‘suspected of being Communist spies,’ while he still talked wildly on, bent single-mindedly on begging them off.
At the time it never once entered my head that this Master Cheng, one of the ‘Four Great Dan,’ had already ‘leaned to the left’—nay, had already ‘toppled over’ altogether.
The brigade-attached officer, Lieutenant Colonel Bai Jiaqi, in the fortieth year of the Republic published serially in the Hong Kong magazine “Guohun” a piece titled “The Battle of Moxingling.”

Its matter told of the throng of refugees who had fled the mainland to Hong Kong, and of a bout of open strife and hidden struggle with the Communist ruffians—of which no more here; but in the text there is a song, having much the savor of that old line, “For valor among the warriors of the Three Kingdoms, Zhao Zilong stands first.” I append it below, as a prelude to the fight at “Lishuiqiao.” The young Tian Yingjie, a goodly son of the House of Han; in letters schooled and schooled in arms, his aim and measure past the common; with both hands he shot in linked succession, and men called him the General of the Double Gun.

The Communist Party rose in revolt, and wrath filled his breast to the brim; in a fury he went off to the army, for pacification and the guard of the nation’s bounds. In the old capital’s northern suburb lies the famed Lishui township; leading his assault team, he garrisoned this quarter. The Communist army came by stealth to raid, its force great and its fury wild; but that good Captain Tian, careful of heart and bolder yet of gall, lay hid to spring the ambush, biding his time and making no sound; and when the Communist army, fierce and frenzied, walked sure enough into the net, at a word of command the men in ambush fired as one, and the Communist army scattered like rats, half fleeing, half fallen dead or hurt. His officers gave him special praise, his brothers were merry and glad, the village elders offered oxen and wine, rejoicing deeply to have won a shield; and all for this one battle—by one battle his fame rang out, the Communist army drew in its head and dared bluster no more; and from that day the Lishui township became a township of great peace.

Under the “North-Suburb Mixed Group” there was a somewhat special “intelligence squad.” The charge of this squad did not lie wholly in the gathering of intelligence; owing to the needs of the actual case, it was furnished besides with a full array of arms, wherewith to deal with the military-district forces that came down from the northern hill country—those belonging to the Chinese Communist “Jin-Cha-Ji Military District” under Nie Rongzhen’s command—and with the militia brigades of the neighboring townships. This squad was set up in the village of “Lishuiqiao” in Daxing county, and was directed near at hand by the North-Suburb Mixed Group stationed at “Zhaojiafen”; the leader of the “North-Suburb Group” was first Chang Shaozeng, and after him Feng Yuzhu. The squad leader of the “intelligence squad” was Tian Yingjie, the very “Captain Tian” whom the brigade-attached Lieutenant Colonel Bai Jiaqi sang. How, then, did the “squad leader” come to be a “captain”? In the piece “The Battle of Lishuiqiao” furnished by my fellow-student Tian Yingjie there is an explanation; the whole text is woven of blood and tears, and grips the heart.

“Lishuiqiao” is a village, with something over three hundred households; in the midst of the village runs a river, and over the river was built a cement bridge, whence it took its name. This place had no national-army garrison, and the Chinese Communist militia came and went there often; some too call a place of this kind a “gray zone.” Now let us look at the original text of my fellow-student Tian Yingjie.—“The place where the fighting fell out was ‘Lishuiqiao’ in Daxing county, some thirty li or so from the Andingmen of Beiping.

“‘The dwellers in the village were three hundred households and more, which counts for a fairly large one. In the middle of the village runs a river, and over the river a great bridge built of cement. Taking this for the base point, due south there is a broad and straight cobbled highroad, leading through to Andingmen; northward one may reach the counties of Changping and Huairou. It may be called, then, a thoroughfare for going in and out of Beiping. Near the bridge were a general store, a little eating-house, and a tea-shed; but of a larger scale were two great distilleries (liquor works). Not far from the bridge stood a temple, which, the times being hard, could no longer keep its incense-fires burning bright.

“‘Of these two great distilleries but one now remained; the other, for the bad times, had closed its business, its works standing empty—and these came just right to serve as a very fair barracks. It is said that national-army troops had several times been garrisoned here, but never for long: all were swallowed up by the Communist army in the fashion of the big eating the small. Down to now there had been, for a year and more, no national-army troops garrisoned here at all.

“‘In truth, ‘Lishuiqiao,’ for Beiping, ought to hold a place of no small importance; but alas, it had now become a ‘district of the three unmanaged,’ and especially when night came it lay wellnigh wholly under the Communist army’s control—wherein there is much that is hard to fathom.

“‘In the winter of the thirty-sixth year my First Pacification Brigade set up the ‘North-Suburb Group’; its leader Chang Shaozeng led the group and was stationed at ‘Zhaojiafen.’ Relying on the whole group’s efforts by day and by night, and taking the way of mustering and drilling the localities, step by step and village by village we gradually recovered ground and pushed forward; and by the spring of the thirty-seventh year we had advanced our post to ‘Yangshan.’ At that time the group leader Chang Shaozeng was transferred to work with the ‘West-Suburb Group,’ and the post of leader passed to Feng Yuzhu. Under the leadership of the two group leaders, Chang and Feng, and by the common efforts of twenty-odd young members, in a state where there were officers but no rank and file and all set to together, in the space of four or five months we had advanced from the suburbs of Beiping into the territory of Daxing county.

“‘What we met with were the Chinese Communist ‘village cadres,’ ‘militia,’ ‘guerrilla bands,’ and the ‘military-district forces’ that had a fixed establishment; that we were able to strike root and gain a footing at ‘Lishuiqiao’ was, in truth, no easy-won thing.

“‘In view of the lessons of the past, and of the needs of the actual case, the higher authority enlarged the ‘intelligence squad’ under the ‘North-Suburb Group’ into an ‘assault team,’ still in Yingjie’s charge. In the early days the team’s members were a dozen and more, with an equipment of three American submachine guns, six carbines, and four Canadian pistols.

“‘Developing by degrees, first at ‘Lishuiqiao’ we helped that village set up a self-defense corps of twenty men, and went on to set up self-defense forces in the other villages of Daxing county too—though these ran but three or five men apiece, mustered over the whole county they came to a hundred and more. Through our guidance and our arming, they were formed into a brigade, and the county engaged Liu Ziyuan as its brigade commander. Liu Ziyuan had formerly been of the old following of the ‘North China Loyal and Patriotic Army,’ and because of this bond it was the easier for all to work in one heart together.
“‘Our own small assault team was but a dozen men and more, yet over the Daxing county self-defense brigade, which outnumbered us several times over, it still played the leading part.

“‘The Daxing county self-defense brigade should, properly speaking, be reckoned a civilian self-defense force recognized by the county government. The brigade still went by the three-tier system, with three company commanders under it, all seasoned old hands at guerrilla work, and under the companies were many squad leaders besides. As for arms and equipment, scraped and pieced together they had in all two light machine guns, two grenade-launchers, and a hundred-odd long and short guns of assorted makes—in short, every man of the corps had a gun. And under the brigade commander Liu Ziyuan’s whipping into shape they had come to look quite the part. As for the supply of grain and pay, in principle each raised its own and all was issued out in common. Looked at merely from the angle of a village self-defense corps, of which no high demands are made, it might be counted a very good body of men.

“‘This body’s greatest peculiarity lay in its round of work and rest, which differed from the common: they rested by day in the barracks, doing some indoor lessons of their own choosing, and were on no account allowed to show themselves abroad; from the moment darkness fell they went out on duty by turns, and, save in some special case, returned to post before the light of dawn. The reason for so doing was that not only could strangers from without make nothing of us, but even the local folk could not make out our numbers or our arms—knowing at the most that troops were stationed here, and seeing but two sentries at the gate.

“‘Besides this, in the thirty or forty villages great and small round about ‘Lishuiqiao’ there were unarmed civilian organizations—youth teams, boys’ teams and children’s corps, women’s teams, and the like—and their tasks were each apportioned: the youth teams had charge of the sentry-posts at the village mouths; the boys’ teams had charge of carrying letters, which were graded by their required speed into three kinds—the ordinary, the urgent with a chicken-feather added, and the most-urgent with a matchstick tied on. The women’s teams had charge of examining or visiting the guests at every household. All these doings were dispatched severally by the baojia office.
“‘These, then, are a brief sketch of our work after we entered ‘Lishuiqiao.’

“‘On the ninth day of the tenth month of the thirty-seventh year, Yingjie (so the author of this piece styles himself) left the corps at midday and went abroad; and after inspecting the duty at the several villages, toward four in the afternoon I turned in at the corps headquarters in Fuxue Hutong within the city. Because on the morrow, the Double Tenth, the headquarters was to hold a mass wedding, and among the bridegrooms were my good friends Zhuang Fei, Yang Tianduo, Zhang Yuesheng, and others—though I could not be present, I must needs offer my congratulations; so I first signed my name in the register the guard squad had made ready, and begged the squad leader Li Zhida to convey my regards for me.

“‘Just as I was making ready to leave the corps and return to post, word came that the unit commander summoned me, and so, of course, I could not go. Commander Chen questioned me on many matters of the local state of things. As I took my leave I met the political instructor Luo besides, and talked over somewhat the life of the brothers within the group; and by the time I hurried to Andingmen to go out of the city, it wanted but two or three minutes of the closing of the gate—it was well I was known to the guard on duty, or I could not have escaped another round of questioning.

“‘Passing by ‘Zhaojiafen,’ I looked in as I went upon the self-defense corps’ captain Lu. He told me that my mother had come to see me, and had passed this way—hurry back, he said. When I hastened back to ‘Lishuiqiao’ it was already near nine o’clock. At the meeting of mother and son there was, of course, no avoiding a spell of homely talk. When I had settled the old lady comfortably, and came to the council room to make ready the apportioning of tonight’s work, the brigade commander Liu Ziyuan and the other party-leaders were already long in their seats. As chance would have it, at this very juncture word came from without that ‘there was a situation.’ Of late such situations were frequent, and by the wonted usage a small party of men was always sent out to have a look; and so it was this time, no exception. But when the report came back again, all was wrong: every sentry-post of our village had vanished without shadow or trace, gone none knew whither—this was bad indeed. At once we set the ranks in order and made ready to give battle, first sending out three parties, each of a dozen men or so, in three columns toward the east, the south, and the west, to a probing counter-thrust. About ten minutes later, from every column a great din of gunfire arose, louder to the ear than the welcoming of the God of Wealth on the second of the first month; and before long the brothers of the three columns had mostly fallen back severally, and among them were some who had ‘taken color.’

“‘By now it was just ten o’clock at night, and by our judgment we were already encircled. To all seeming the bandit army would straightway press a general assault. After taking counsel with the brigade commander Liu Ziyuan, we resolved on the one hand to make within the village a ‘fixed-point return of fire,’ set with automatic rifles, light machine guns, and submachine guns of strong firepower; and on the other to send out guerrilla parties to draw off the bandit army and scatter its strength—this holding too a purpose of laying a false show, so that the other side could not make out where our main body lay. At the same time we sent up signal flares to warn the concerned units near by and to call for aid.

“‘As to the lie of things within and without: the whole village of ‘Lishuiqiao’ had three hundred households and more, of which a certain number had, in the hidden parts of their woodsheds and cattle-byres, set up passages by which one might pass through from one to another. Without: due south of ‘Lishuiqiao,’ five li off, was the barracks of ‘Beiyuan,’ where a battalion of the 208th Division was stationed, their charge being only the management of recruits. Five li to the southwest was ‘Lujiafen,’ where were stationed some forty men and more under the self-defense captain Lu Huanzhong. Two or three li further southwest was our own ‘North-Suburb Mixed Group,’ stationed at ‘Yangshan.’ Due east, eight li off, at ‘Yongshiying,’ were some thirty men and more of a self-defense corps.

“‘After our signals went up, from all the quarters above there seemed to be some response, yet it was not marked, and by our reckoning the hope was faint. Looking at the time, another thirty minutes had passed, and it was now half past ten at night. Within the village there was not a caw nor a chirp, all utterly still; the children must all have fallen asleep, for not a sound of weeping could be heard.

“‘Minute by minute, second by second, a little while more went by, when of a sudden a streak of red flashed in the sky, and hard upon it, from every side and quarter, a killing-cry that stunned the ear: the bandit army’s assault had begun. This was a thing looked for; there was no choice but to keep one’s composure!

“‘The gunfire round about rose here and fell there; and beyond the one great cry of slaughter, the village was quiet no more—grown folk shouting, children wailing, all thrown into a tangle, which truly disturbed the temper. We few who bore the charge of command warned one another, over and over, that we must at all costs hold our nerve.

“‘By now the guerrilla parties sent out before, though they had done their work of holding the enemy in check, seemed to have found cover in the lie of the ground and its features, and had for the time halted their advance and set their ranks in order. Taking the whole case, they had already drawn the ring of encirclement tighter, and the room in which we could move grew smaller and smaller. The gunfire came in bursts, now and again, and the firepower of our outer ring waned by degrees, as though it could hold out no longer. By this point, though both sides, ours and the enemy’s, must surely have had their dead and wounded, yet the enemy being many and we few, to wear on so would turn ever more against us.

“‘Looking at the time, it was already past one in the small hours of the tenth of October; the fighting had gone on, all told, two hours and more; no aid from without had reached our side; the enemy clung close and would not let go; and if we could not break out before the light of dawn, the thing was past all bearing to think of. In a flash there rose in me, all at once, a contradictory thought: because our firepower was strong and held the overwhelming advantage, I found myself rather hoping the other side would attack right in, so as first to sap their fighting strength, and then it would be the easier to break out; yet were it so, the women and children and the old of the village must needs suffer the ravage—and where then would my heart find peace?

“‘After discussion, we resolved at last to break out. Before breaking out, we first sent to the several guerrilla parties the signal for an ‘urgent concentration,’ and a few minutes later, save for one party whose case was unknown, the other four parties, happily wounded but with none dead, all came back. So we set ourselves in order once more, and Yingjie and the brigade commander Liu Ziyuan, each leading his own men, divided into two columns and, following the favorable ground, began the action of breaking out.

“‘In an instant, all through ‘Lishuiqiao,’ within the village and without, the single-shot report of rifles, the burst of hand grenades, the strung-bead rattle of light machine guns wove themselves into one wild and thundering din. More hateful still was the bandit army’s assault upon the mind—crying aloud: ‘Give up your guns! Give up your guns and you shall not die; take them alive!’ and, pausing a moment, crying again: ‘Captain Tian is caught—come and see!’ In ordinary times we had taught the brothers how to understand the enemy’s ‘crying-out before the lines,’ and so the brothers might not be moved by it; yet the heart of a mother’s son—if my mother heard it in her ears, how could the old lady’s heart not ache?

“‘We had agreed beforehand that, after breaking out each his own way, we should muster at ‘Yangfang,’ three li to the southwest of ‘Lishuiqiao.’ Should the case not allow it, then each was to make his own choice for safety.

“‘To speak now of the equipment I, Yingjie, bore upon me: in my hand was a submachine gun, with five magazines to it; at my waist was strapped a German-made No. 3 pistol; and I carried besides two American hand grenades. My one thought at the time was simply to fight it out. ‘From the taking of the break-out action at two in the dead of night, because there was no light in the dark, a watch was as good as none, and I lost by degrees my own command of the time—which is to say, I could not clearly tell how long had passed. In that space I went through two charges; the formation fell into utter disorder; and as I moved on I could not even see a single man to left or right. Yet at my back I heard the whole village given over to a din of great weeping and little crying, and could not but feel a pang of grief.

“‘For my own part, to move alone and single was rather the more convenient; and, save for my care over the whole case and the plight of the brothers, I kept myself as steady and cool as I could. I understood too that the other side’s way of fighting was this: they bawled fiercely with their mouths, but where they could not fix a target they would on no account lightly fire. And so my chances were the more.

“‘By now two of the submachine gun’s magazines were spent, and three were left; I dodged aside and crouched down, listened a while, changed the magazine in the dark by feel, and went on alone. On and on I went, when ahead there seemed a great heap of something writhing; drawing near and listening close, I heard a panting, gasping sound, as though several men were twisted into one knot, wrangling over some one thing—but who and who was this? For the moment I could not make it out. Steadying myself, I listened a while more—ah! now I had it: it was our machine-gunner, seized fast in another’s arms, three or four men striving to wrest the gun from his gripping, unyielding hands, while the machine-gunner, come what might, would not let go. On the instant, at a height of about two meters above the ground, tu-tu-tu, tu-tu-tu, I loosed off half a magazine of rounds toward them; and those men, in the frame of mind that takes every bush and tree for a soldier, were startled into flight.
“‘Why did I fire two meters above the ground? I feared to hit one of our own men.

“‘The machine-gunner and I hid that somewhat unwieldy machine gun beneath the sweet-potato vines, to come back and fetch it when the chance offered. We reckoned that we were now no more than two or three hundred meters out of the village, and had still to press southward. Just as we were about to set off, of a sudden I heard voices right ahead, and no small number of them: plainly our way onward was already barred. Turning it over—to the left, to the right, there seemed no way to slip clear; perhaps the most dangerous road, the way back, might hold a brief safety. So the machine-gunner and I, the two of us, drew a long space apart, turned about, and went northward. Past all expectation, the whole way was quiet, and we got back very smoothly to the bridgehead. Over the bridge lay the village. When I was but some ten or twenty paces off from that cement bridge, I lay flat to the ground, and, listening and looking together, took careful measure once more, and made sure there was no one on the bridge; then, growing bold, I drew near the bridgehead. I stopped, picked up a clod of earth and threw it into the river; there was a sound, but not loud; I waited a space, and there was no response; whereon I stepped quickly up onto the bridge, thinking it were best if I could clear it at a bound.

“‘Just as I was nearing the halfway point of the bridge floor—disaster! all at once a man sprang out and asked the ‘password.’ To shrink back now was too late; there was nothing for it but to answer, all mumbled and blurred, a single ‘a-ha’—what those two sounds were, in truth, not even I myself knew; yet in that very instant of the other’s hesitation I had darted to the north end of the bridge. Past all expectation, several men closed round me, bawling at me to raise my hands; and with a single cry of ‘Right—!’ I let fly a whole magazine of rounds all at once, and how many of them lay down, I do not know.

“‘Just as I was about to get clear, worse befell: the collar of the greatcoat I wore was already gripped by a man at my side, and another came up meaning to seize me in his arms. No sooner said than done—I drove the muzzle-end of my submachine gun at the head of the man who gripped my collar; and though he gave a great cry and fell to the ground, still his hand would not let go, and he all but dragged me down with him. It was well that the collar was all snap-buttons; a few wrenches and I tore free. At the same time I swung the submachine gun round in a sweep, and the man who had meant to seize me was flung off too. One crisis, at the last, was got through.

“‘This happened some three or five meters past the bridge. I went on along the left of the approach-way, and had not gone far when, on the right of the road, a band of men crowded up all at once; and just as I made to fire—the chamber was empty, my rounds were all shot away! My heart lurched in a panic, my step went unsteady, and, with my sight grown dim besides, I set one foot down unsure and, past my own will, tumbled into a trench. This trench we ourselves had dug some days before in a field exercise; it was quite deep, sheer up and sheer down, and no easy thing to climb out of. After I had fallen in, I first knelt at the trench-bottom and changed in a fresh magazine, then took a grenade from my person, pulled the fuse as my hand went, gripped it, drew a breath, evened out my breathing, and made ready to loose it on the instant. By now those above still jeered without cease: ‘Where do you think you’re running now—surrender, quick!’ and then cried again: ‘Quick, throw down your gun, hands up and surrender!’ With a great roar of ‘Here it comes!’ I first flung out the grenade, and hard upon it, treading hard against the jagged, uneven ridges of the trench, sprang upward; and from where that surge of strength came I cannot tell, but my upper body was already thrust out beyond the trench, clinging fast to its lip; and heedless whether the angle were right or no, I let fly one fierce volley. Strange to tell, under the cover of that leveled hail of fire I had already leapt out of the trench and onto the highroad.

“‘Careless whether there were men near by or none, I gathered all my strength and ran. I knew that not far ahead there was a ruined blockhouse, and in it there must surely be men too; this was the last pass, and could I but break through it, thereafter there might perhaps be a turn for the better. As I ran I made ready: first I took off the magazine to check how many rounds were left—heavens! not a single one remained. There was nothing for it but to draw my last treasure—the pistol; but alas, it had only one magazine, six rounds. I reckoned in my heart that I had but five I could use, for the one that remained I must, come what might, keep for myself.

“‘My running legs were weak and clumsy, when I struck against a broken brick and all but tripped and fell. This stumble gave me a hint: I picked up the brick, slung my gun well, and pressed on. By now I was no more than twenty or thirty paces from the blockhouse, when sure enough someone challenged, ‘Pass...word,’ and I answered low; and I had already made out a man standing outside the blockhouse to bar my way. At once I hurled the brick with all my force at him; feeling something flung his way, and while he dodged and swayed, bang, bang, several shots in a row—I had already rushed past and taken to my heels. This time they did fire, but they could not hit me.

“‘In one breath I ran wellnigh a li, then dropped down where I was beside a little grave-mound, and lay flat on the ground outright, resting and panting together while I laid my plans. By now there was still gunfire at ‘Lishuiqiao,’ but not so thick as before. I thought a while, and resolved to go first to ‘Baijiafen’; crossing a shallow river, one came to ‘Yangfang,’ the place we had agreed upon. There I would wait till all were gathered, and then take counsel again.

“‘When I came to the riverbank I fell to hesitating again: I had heard in ordinary times that the water was not deep, but because I could not swim I had never gone down into it, and should the water chance to be over my head, there would be a fine to-do. So I thought; yet in the end I took off my outer coat, wrapped the submachine gun well and shouldered it, and tried stepping into the river. It would not do—I could not keep my footing—and I came back to the bank, meaning to find a stick, so that, like a blind man, I might feel out the way with it as I went, which would be much better. I sought a good while and could find none; then in a flash of wit I broke off a tree-branch, stripped away its leaves, and made shift with it. Happily the river was truly not deep, not up to my chest, and I waded across very easily.

“‘It was well that I was wet only below the waist; the weather, though somewhat cold, left my upper body still warm. I checked the rounds in my pistol—only two were left; should I meet with another situation, it would go hard with me.

“‘Walking and resting by turns, I was already worn past bearing. With great toil, step by step, I dragged myself to ‘Yangfang’—but there was not so much as a shadow of a man. On second thoughts: the sky was already whitening toward the east, and no one would have waited until now. I skirted ‘Yangfang,’ and turned to make straight for ‘Lujiafen.’ All at once I caught sight of a file of troops moving at a run from south to north; and since I could not be sure whether they were foe or friend, I could only lie down and hide myself a space. Only afterward did I learn that it was in fact the self-defense corps of ‘Lujiafen.’

“‘When that file had passed, I stood up and went on; and not far from ‘Lujiafen’ I heard someone ahead cry the ‘password’ again. This time I was not alarmed, for I could tell it was the voice of my fellow-student Mi Renfu of our ‘North-Suburb Mixed Group.’ When I answered aloud and drew near, it was indeed my two fellow-students Mi Renfu and Ma Liangzhi; and at meeting we were beyond measure glad. Just as we were about to tell over what had passed, we saw a military truck coming toward us on the highroad; and by the word of my two fellow-students Mi and Ma, the group leader Feng Yuzhu had already gone into the city to seek aid—this might well be the relief.
“‘Before long I heard the sound of cannon again. It must be that our own regular troops too had come out to the relief, for in this tract only our own regular army had cannon.

“‘Still I could not set my mind at rest over ‘Lishuiqiao,’ whose case was unknown. Taking counsel with my fellow-student Ma Liangzhi, I first handed him my submachine gun, empty of rounds, to carry back for me, and begged him further to oblige me by lending me for the while the carbine he carried. I had meant to drink a mouthful of water, but could not even wait for that; in all haste I turned about and hurried back, now walking, now running along the way, and the day had broken, and ‘Lishuiqiao’ was already before my eyes. The first I came upon was a body of horse of the ‘Fourth Cavalry Division of the North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters.’ I went forward to declare who I was; but in this sorry plight of mine, save for a single carbine, I had nothing about me to serve as proof. The cavalry troops, half believing and half doubting, took me with them into the village.
“‘The first I met was the self-defense captain Liu Ziyuan; and when we had said to each other the word of ‘well-toiled,’ we set about looking over the dead and wounded and putting the ranks in order.

To turn back now to the ‘North-Suburb Group’ leader Feng Yuzhu: from the moment he perceived, the night before, that things were amiss on the side of ‘Lishuiqiao,’ he had meant to bring a few of his fellow-students and, joining with the ‘Lujiafen’ self-defense corps, come up to the rescue; but on making inquiry many times, the case being always unclear, it was very hard to come to a quick decision, and to venture rashly on the thing he feared might be ill-judged. So through the night he sought leave to go into the city, and laid an urgent report before the brigade headquarters.

“‘The deputy unit commander Mr. Li Yulin, on receiving the group leader Feng’s report, at once put himself in touch with the ‘North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,’ and so a battalion (short one company) of the ‘Fourth Cavalry Division’ was sent out to lend its aid. At this moment the deputy unit commander Li, together with a staff-officer of the Third Section of the ‘North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,’ was come in person to ‘Lishuiqiao’ to learn the true state of things.
“‘When I met with the deputy unit commander Li, past our own will we fell into each other’s arms; and the deputy unit commander Li said: ‘You’re back. That is well.’

He forthwith drew me over and presented me to that staff-officer of the Bandit-Suppression Headquarters, who also gave me a word of comfort and cheer. Then I asked leave of the deputy unit commander Li, and went to the house of old Mrs. Liu to visit my mother.

“‘My mother is a strong and kindly old woman; and when we, mother and son, met, the old lady gripped my two hands tight and was long silent, not knowing what were best to say; yet the inmost feelings of the two of us, mother and son, must surely both have been warm. I am the only son of the House of Tian, and now, working a year in the North Suburb, I had not once been home; my mother, yearning for her son, would come every month or two to look upon him, and by ill chance she had lit upon this day’s scene. My mother’s very first words to me were: ‘Mother knew you would come to no harm.’ And, stroking my face with her hand, she said again: ‘Go quickly to your work; go quickly and look to the other brothers—they are still waiting for you to care for them!’ ‘The first results of the reckoning on the spot: of the Daxing self-defense corps, eleven dead and twenty-seven wounded, light and grave; of the assault team (the intelligence squad) that I led, one dead, one missing, and three wounded, light and grave.

“‘Liu Ziyuan reported that the light machine gun we had hidden away had been found, but that some of the brothers’ rifles were lost. Captain Liu further begged the deputy unit commander Li that the wounded of the corps might, under the name of the ‘0760’ unit, be sent to a military hospital for treatment. When this batch of wounded reached the brigade headquarters, it was the very hour when our own unit’s ten couples were holding their Double-Tenth mass wedding ceremony. The infirmary put the self-defense corps’ wounded into military uniform, fitted them besides with the ‘0760’ insignia, and passed them on to the field hospital.

“‘To speak again of the side of ‘Lishuiqiao’: at this time the medical orderlies with the cross on their backs, sent by the ‘North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters,’ together with the porters levied by the baojia office, were burying the fallen of our self-defense corps. The corps-men were not all of them local people, and most had not even any family. Whether after death there was any little grant of condolence, I fear it does not bear speaking of; and it was the same even with the men of our assault team. As for the dead and wounded of the side we had fought, the corpses dredged up from where they had been flung into the several wells came to some thirty-odd; more pitiful yet to see was the washing of the bloodstains from the doors and windows and walls, where now and again there were scraps of limbs besides—this is what is called flesh and blood flying in all directions. Two hours later, the ‘civilian porters,’ some dozens of them, whom the bandit soldiers had seized out of the village, came back too, by degrees. By their account, they had been seized at past three in the night, first gathered together in the great temple of the baojia office, and then set to carry off, on stretchers made of door-planks torn down, some of the gravely wounded, to go along with them. There were besides several rubber-wheeled, man-hauled handcarts from the households, on which they loaded the corpses and the lightly wounded. Afterward, when it was near dawn, hearing the sound of cannon, they took fright; and one ‘cadre’ passed the order to stuff all the gravely wounded into the wells, and would have no more of the handcarts. So on the road leading from ‘Lishuiqiao’ to ‘Xiegezhuang’ there were again many heaps of dead bodies.

“‘Those men who had been pressed into porterage said further that when they reached ‘Xiegezhuang’ they were let go and sent back. As for whither the bandit army went, they did not know—which, I suppose, was the very reason they were set free.

“‘Further, by the word of the soldiers of the Bandit-Suppression Headquarters’ Fourth Cavalry Division, they had picked up some articles the bandit army had cast away: besides a small quantity of broken weapons, there were a hundred-odd military caps of different makes.

“‘Afterward, the intelligence showed that the bandit army which had come to the attack on the ninth of October belonged to three newly-formed militia brigades of the ‘Jin-Ji-Cha Military District,’ their whole strength some 1,100-odd men, of whom a part were bare-handed. And herein too was found an answer: namely, why they had been so loath to fire.

“‘In the several months thereafter the enlarged assault team went on still, active in every village of this tract, a score of li and more about.’ So much for the ‘Battle of Lishuiqiao’ set down by my fellow-student Tian Yingjie. In the very last passage of the whole text the writer has laid a slight hand, leaving out a few phrases of the pitiful scene of the battlefield there depicted, that the reek of slaughter might not be too heavy.
